L262: # Superior vena cava obstruction
L263: ## Overview
L264: The superior vena cava (SVC) is the second largest vein in your body, carrying deoxygenated blood from the upper half of your body to the right atrium, which is one of the four chambers in your heart. SVC obstruction occurs when the vein becomes narrowed or blocked. SVC obtruction can occur in chest tumours or enlarged lymph nodes, leading to external compression of the SVC.
L265: The obstruction may be a chronic condition, meaning it lasts for a long time, or it may be acute, meaning the condition starts suddenly and lasts for a short time.
L266: In most cases, the cause of the obstruction is cancer, particularly lung cancer, although not all of the possible causes are cancerous.
L267: ## Symptoms
L268: 
L269: The main symptom is shortness of breath. Other symptoms include a cough, headaches, swelling of the face, neck or arms, and swelling of veins in the neck, chest or arms.
L270: 
L271: ## Diagnosis
L272: 
L273: A doctor can diagnose the condition using imaging techniques, such as contrast-enhanced 【164†CT】, 【165†MRI】 or a technique called a digital subtraction angiography.
L274: ## Treatment
L275: 
L276: If the obstruction in the vein is caused by cancer, it is usually treated with radiation therapy and chemotherapy. However, it may take several weeks for the patient to respond to these treatments.
L277: 【166†SVC stenting】 is a safe and effective procedure in which an interventional radiologist places a metal stent into the narrowed or blocked vein to hold it open. It is a minimally invasive option which can be carried out as a stand-alone procedure or in addition to other treatments. SVC stenting can be performed under general anaesthesia or mild sedation. A stent is a tube woven of thin metal wires. Stents are available in different length and sizes.
L278: By access via a vein in the groin or neck, a plastic tube called a catheter and a thin wire are used to pass the narrowing of the vessel. Afterwards, a stent is positioned under fluoroscopic guidance. Sometimes the stent has to be pushed to vessel wall by using a small balloon which is inflated inside the stent. In case of long stenosis two or more stents are positioned to bypass vessel narrowing In most cases, symptoms will clear up quickly following the stent placement, usually within 24 to 48 hours.
L279: Theain procedure risks are stent migration to the right heart, stent defect, and obturation of the SVC.

L164@P2: (2). Les options thérapeutiques en cas de sténose de la VCS sont le pontage chirurgical, le
L165@P2: traitement de revascularisation par ballonnet et
L166@P2: endoprothèse ou, éventuellement, une thrombectomie percutanée dirigée par cathéter (2).
L167@P2: En somme, la localisation pariétale abdominale inhabituelle des varices n’évoque pas d’emblée, dans ce cas, un SVCS ni une hypertension
L168@P2: portale, mais l’imagerie démontre l’anastomose
L169@P2: entre les systèmes caves supérieurs et inférieurs. En revanche, les antécédents médicaux
L170@P2: du patient représentent un indicateur important.
L171@P2: Les cliniciens devraient, dès lors, garder en
L172@P2: mémoire la possibilité d’une présentation pariétale abdominale de SVCS, particulièrement chez
L173@P2: les patients ayant subi un cathétérisme veineux
L174@P2: central même plusieurs années auparavant. Un
L175@P2: SVCS peut en effet se présenter dans une situation d’urgence.
L176@P2: Depuis la dernière consultation de chirurgie,
L177@P2: aucune indication thérapeutique pour la sténose
L178@P2: veineuse cave supérieure n’a été posée, mais
L179@P2: le patient n’a toutefois pas été éligible pour une
L180@P2: plastie abdominale afin de ne pas altérer la circulation veineuse collatérale et risquer de compromettre le retour veineux vers l’oreillette droite.
L181@P2: Implication clinique
L182@P2: L’observation de varicosités de localisation
L183@P2: inhabituelle à la paroi abdominale doit notamment faire évoquer un syndrome de la veine
L184@P2: cave supérieure, en particulier chez les patients
L185@P2: ayant des antécédents de cathétérisme veineux
L186@P2: central, même plusieurs années auparavant.
L187@P2: Les symptômes d’une compression de la
L188@P2: veine cave supérieure peuvent être tardifs et
L189@P2: se révéler dans un contexte d’urgence médicochirurgicale. Une anamnèse soignée et une
L190@P2: réflexion générale lors de l’examen clinique sont
L191@P2: essentielles pour orienter l’exploration complémentaire. Une imagerie tomodensitométrique
L192@P2: thoraco-abdominale permettra de préciser le
L193@P2: diagnostic afin de discuter du traitement approprié, mais également d’éviter toute intervention
L194@P2: chirurgicale risquant d’altérer le retour veineux
L195@P2: vers l’oreillette droite.
L196@P2: Les choix thérapeutiques en cas d’obstruction
L197@P2: de la veine cave supérieure sont un pontage
L198@P2: chirurgical, un traitement de revascularisation
L199@P2: par ballonnet et endoprothèse ou, éventuellement, une thrombectomie percutanée dirigée
L200@P2: par cathéter.
L201@P2: Conclusion
L202@P2: Le SVCS est un tableau clinique qui résulte
L203@P2: d’une obstruction de la VCS. Les cathéters
L204@P2: veineux centraux et les CVCI peuvent favoriser l’apparition d’un SVCS par des lésions
L205@P2: endovasculaires et une thrombose de la VCS.
L206@P2: Les cliniciens devraient être conscients des
L207@P2: présentations pariétales abdominales inhabituelles d’un SVCS, en particulier chez les
L208@P2: patients ayant subi un cathétérisme veineux
L209@P2: central même plusieurs années auparavant.
L210@P2: Un SVCS peut devenir une situation urgente
L211@P2: nécessitant un traitement spécifique ou contreindiquant certaines interventions chirurgicales.
L212@P2: En cas de suspicion de SVCS, une exploration par tomodensitométrie thoraco-abdominale
L213@P2: devrait être réalisée en complément d’un avis
L214@P2: chirurgical cardio-vasculaire.

L260: # Vena cava stenting
L261: ## What is vena cava stenting?
L262: 
L263: A stent is a metal mesh tube. Vena cava stents are designed for use in the superior vena cava (SVC), which transports deoxygenated blood from the upper part of the body back to the heart. In rarer cases they are used in the 【163†inferior vena cava (IVC)】, which carries the deoxygenated blood from the lower part of the body back to the heart.
L264: Vena cava stenting is used to manage a stenosis (narrowing) or blockage in the vein, which is most commonly caused by a malignant (cancerous) tumour. The procedure may be recommended if you are in an emergency situation, but this depends on your clinical symptoms.
L265: 
L266: 【164†Image】
L267: ## How does the procedure work?
L268: 
L269: The interventional radiologist will insert a 3 mm plastic tube (called a sheath) into the base of your skull or your groin. They will then guide the sheath near to the stenosis or blockage in the affected vein. The vein will be reopened using a metallic wire and a selective catheter using a technique called recanalisation, after which the vena cava stent is placed.
L270: The stent is self-expanding and acts like a skeleton to keep the vena cava open. If your vena cava is completely blocked due to a tumour, your interventional radiologist may also insert a tiny balloon which inflates once it is in the vein before and after inserting the stent. You will need to take medication that prevents blood clotting for 1-2 weeks following the procedure; the exact time period depends on the type of stent used and your clinical situation.
L271: 
L272: 【165†Image】
L273: ## Why perform it?
L274: 
L275: The aim of vena cava stenting is to manage symptoms caused by an obstruction of the blood flow in the vein, which is much more common in the SVC than in the IVC.
L276: 
L277: The main symptom of an obstructed blood flow in the vena cava is shortness of breath, followed by swelling of the face, neck or arms, a headache, a cough and enlargement of the veins in the neck, chest and arms. You may experience other symptoms but they are rare.
L278: Your symptoms should stop within 48 hours of the stent placement.
L279: ## What are the risks?
L280: 
L281: There are some minor risks, including the risk of infection and bruising at the puncture site in your neck or groin. Major risks include the risk of the stent accidentally going into the heart during placement, the development of a blood clot, or the stent later becoming blocked due to a tumour, though in this case the vessel can be reopened in a second intervention.
